final_recommendation: The room converged on a trilateral package: 15-year term with year-10 review, 75% auto RVC with 70/72/75 supplier phase-in, binding transparency clause requiring Mexico to publish corrective orders within 30 days, dairy quotas locked (6,500 cheese, 2,200 milk powder, 1,500 yogurt), and auto-extend mechanism with focused corrective windows replacing hard sunset. Canada signed contingent on Chapter 19 preservation (assumed but not explicitly negotiated in transcript). Congressional ratification risk remains elevated but addressable.
minority_objections: Labor unions initially demanded day-one 75% compliance with no supplier phase-in, rejected in favor of 70/72/75 glide path
Dairy agriculture threatened to withdraw congressional support if Canada didn't commit specific tonnage caps immediately
Supply chain manufacturers warned capex freeze without binding RVC targets in published corrective orders
key_conflicts: Day-one 75% RVC vs. supplier phase-in (resolved via 70/72/75 binding milestones)
Hard 10-year sunset vs. business certainty (resolved via 15-year term with year-10 review and auto-extend)
U.S. unilateral inspections vs. Mexican sovereignty (resolved via third-party auditors with published corrective orders)
Vague dairy access vs. Canadian political constraints (resolved via specific tonnage caps in schedule)
Soft corrective commitments vs. enforceable accountability (resolved via 30-day publication requirement in agreement text)
key_concessions: Mexico accepted binding transparency clause requiring public corrective orders within 30 days
U.S. accepted 70/72/75 supplier phase-in instead of day-one 75% across all tiers
Canada accepted specific dairy tonnage caps (6,500/2,200/1,500) with 10-year review
Mexico accepted non-compliance blocking extension at year-10 review
U.S./Canada accepted auto-extend mechanism with focused corrective windows instead of hard termination
red_lines: Mexico: no U.S. government inspectors in Mexican plants (resolved via third-party auditors)
Canada: Chapter 19 dispute settlement non-negotiable (assumed preserved, not explicitly debated)
Labor: no ratification without enforceable wage-floor compliance mechanism
Congress: no extension without published corrective orders binding Mexico to measurable targets
Auto industry: no capex commitment without elimination of sunset cliff
ignored_or_underweighted_risks: Chapter 19 dispute settlement never explicitly negotiated despite Canada stating it as non-negotiable red line
Enforcement consequences for RVC non-compliance at supplier level remain vague (license suspension vs. tariff vs. notice)
Year-13 corrective timeline creates new cliff if Mexico misses targets
Congressional ratification timeline and vote-counting not discussed
Steel/aluminum tariffs and their interaction with auto rules not addressed
downstream_risk_variables: Third-party auditor selection process and independence verification mechanism undefined
Quarterly audit frequency and unannounced-access protocols not locked down
Year-13 corrective-action failure triggers unknown (does deal lapse or extend again?)
Canada's Chapter 19 preservation assumed but not confirmed in writing
Dairy tonnage-increase mechanism post-year-10 review undefined
Supplier-level enforcement consequences (RVC gaps) remain unspecified
uncertainty_notes: Chapter 19 dispute settlement assumed preserved but never explicitly negotiated. Enforcement mechanism for supplier RVC gaps (vs. wage floors) remains vague. Year-13 corrective failure consequences undefined. Third-party auditor selection and independence protocols not locked. Congressional vote-counting and ratification timeline not discussed.

marker_evidence.auto_rules_bottleneck: 75% RVC day-one vs. supplier phase-in drove R2-R5 impasse; resolved only via binding 70/72/75 milestones with transparency clause — auto industry threatened capex freeze, labor demanded day-one compliance, USTR initially refused phase-in until Mexico/Canada forced compromise
marker_evidence.labor_enforcement_key: Third-party auditors, 30-day corrective-order publication, non-compliance blocking extension, and quarterly enforcement all emerged as binding ratification requirements — labor unions explicitly stated 'my members won't tell Congress to vote yes' without enforceable mechanisms, drove transparency clause into agreement text
marker_evidence.canada_dairy_final_issue: Specific tonnage caps (6,500/2,200/1,500) became Canada's signing condition — dairy agriculture threatened congressional support withdrawal, Canada demanded written schedule before Parliamentary approval, resolved via locked quotas with 10-year review
marker_evidence.dispute_settlement_canada_redline: Canada stated Chapter 19 as 'non-negotiable' and 'Parliament walks if we lose dispute settlement' but it was never actually negotiated or discussed further — mentioned once, then ignored
marker_evidence.sunset_to_review_compromise: Hard 10-year sunset rejected by Canada/industry as 'political coffin' and 'capex-freezing' — drove shift to 15-year term with year-10 review and auto-extend mechanism, explicitly framed as solving business-uncertainty problem
marker_evidence.ratification_risk: Congress repeatedly raised enforcement teeth and transparency as ratification requirements, but actual vote-counting, timeline, or whip strategy never discussed — acknowledged as constraint but did not drive specific concessions beyond enforcement mechanisms
marker_evidence.supply_chain_adjustment: Supply chain manufacturers raised capex freeze, tooling costs, compliance calendar uncertainty, and sourcing reorganization — influenced supplier phase-in compromise but did not block or fundamentally reshape the 75% RVC target itself
marker_evidence.us_mexico_first_pressures_canada: Mexico explicitly stated 'trilateral-or-nothing' and threatened bilateral fallback multiple times — USTR framed U.S.-Mexico deal as fait accompli, forcing Canada to accept dairy caps and auto rules or be excluded, drove Canada's signing decision
